title: Pre-training Limited Memory Language Models with Internal and External Knowledge
claim: Prior approaches add external knowledge on top of a model that still memorizes facts; ours offloads facts to the external store.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, matched blocks, color swap blue vs orange
description: Two side-by-side panels with the same layout. The left panel is titled "LLM + RAG" and is drawn in blue. A large rounded square labeled "Model" holds "Language Competency" and a lighter circular overlap labeled "Internal Knowledge", split by a dashed orange diagonal line. A blue circle labeled "External Knowledge / Database" sits to its right. A single arrow points from the database into the model, so knowledge is only added. The right panel is titled "LMLM" and is drawn in orange. Its model square has a white circular bite cut out, labeled "Limited Internal Knowledge". Two curved arrows run in both directions between the model and the orange "External Knowledge / Database" circle. The change from blue to orange and the carved-out hole are what the eye notices first.
caption: A schematic illustration of LMLM. Unlike RAG (left), which exclusively adds knowledge from external sources, LMLM offloads knowledge from the LLMs to the external database during pre-training.
abstract: Neural language models are black-boxes--both linguistic patterns and factual knowledge are distributed across billions of opaque parameters. This entangled encoding makes it difficult to reliably inspect, verify, or update specific facts. We introduce Limited Memory Language Models (LMLM), a new class of language models that externalizes factual knowledge to external database during pre-training rather than memorizing them. Our pre-training approach strategically masks externally retrieved factual values from the training loss, thereby teaching the model to perform targeted lookups rather than relying on memorization in model weights. Our experiments demonstrate that LMLMs achieve competitive performance compared to significantly larger LLMs on standard benchmarks, while offering the advantages of explicit, editable, and verifiable knowledge bases.
